title: Numbers 33:1–15
context: On the plains of Moab, at the end of forty years, Numbers pauses to record Israel’s journey from Egypt station by station. Moses wrote the list at the LORD’s command. This first section runs from Rameses, the day after the Passover, through the crossing of the sea, Marah, Elim, and Rephidim, to the wilderness of Sinai, matching the route told in Exodus 12–19. A few stations named here appear nowhere else, and the locations of most of them are unknown or debated. Both traditions read the list as theology in the form of a record: God remembered every step of his people’s way, from the night of judgment on Egypt to the mountain where he gave his covenant.

verses.text: These are the journeys of the children of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their armies under the hand of Moses and Aaron.
verses.arminianNotes:
The heading names the journeys of Israel out of Egypt by their armies, under Moses and Aaron. The story of forty years is summarized as a road travelled under appointed leaders.

Arminian readers see a people who repeatedly chose to follow or resist, yet whose journey God still records. The list invites each generation to remember both God’s faithfulness and its own responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s providence ordering the entire course of his people’s history, including its detours. The exodus begins a pilgrimage that he governs from start to finish.

Both traditions read the journey as a pattern for the life of faith, which Hebrews 11:13–16 describes as a pilgrimage toward a better country.

verses.text: Moses wrote the starting points of their journeys by the commandment of the LORD. These are their journeys according to their starting points.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses wrote down the starting points of the journeys at the LORD’s command. God wanted the road remembered.

Arminian readers note that remembrance is a means of renewed trust. Recalling where God has led helps the people choose faithfulness again at the edge of the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God himself commanded the record, a reminder that Scripture preserves what he wills his people to know. Their history is part of his revelation.

Both traditions draw comfort that God keeps account of his people’s wanderings (compare Psalm 56:8), and that no stage of the journey is forgotten.

verses.text: They traveled from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the next day after the Passover, the children of Israel went out with a high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians,
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel set out from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, going out with a high hand in the sight of the Egyptians. The journey begins in open deliverance.

Arminian readers see God’s saving act as the ground of the people’s new life. Redemption comes first, and the call to walk with God follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see salvation as God’s sovereign work done publicly before the enemy. Israel did not slip away in secret; God brought them out triumphantly (compare Exodus 14:8).

Both traditions read the Passover as fulfilled in Christ (1 Corinthians 5:7) and the exodus as a pattern of redemption.

verses.text: while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck among them. The LORD also executed judgments on their gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Egyptians were burying their firstborn whom the LORD had struck, and the LORD executed judgments on their gods. Deliverance for Israel was judgment for Egypt.

Arminian readers note the sobriety of the scene. Pharaoh’s repeated refusals ended in grief, showing the real consequences of resisting God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize the LORD’s triumph over the gods of Egypt (compare Exodus 12:12). The exodus was a contest of worship, and the LORD alone proved to be God.

Both traditions hear here a warning about idolatry and a reminder that salvation and judgment often appear together in Scripture.

verses.text: The children of Israel traveled from Rameses, and encamped in Succoth.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Rameses Israel camped at Succoth. The first step out of Egypt is recorded simply.

Arminian readers note that the first stage of freedom is an act of trust: leaving the familiar for a road not yet seen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same God who struck Egypt now leads Israel step by step. The plain wording reflects the steady hand of providence behind every stage.

Both traditions see the beginning of a long journey in which God’s people must learn daily dependence, as Exodus 13:20–22 shows with the cloud and fire.

verses.text: They traveled from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, which is in the edge of the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Succoth they camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. Egypt lies behind, and the unknown lies ahead.

Arminian readers note that the edge of the wilderness is a place of decision, where faith must take its next step without seeing the end.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God led Israel by a route of his choosing rather than the shortest way (compare Exodus 13:17–18). His wisdom shapes the path.

Both traditions see the wilderness as a place God uses for training and testing, not a sign of his absence.

verses.text: They traveled from Etham, and turned back to Pihahiroth, which is before Baal Zephon, and they encamped before Migdol.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Etham they turned back to Pihahiroth before Baal Zephon and camped before Migdol. The turn seemed to trap them against the sea.

Arminian readers note how the people faced fear when the route appeared to make no sense, and how their trust was tested.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Exodus 14:1–4 presents this turn as God’s deliberate plan to display his glory over Pharaoh. What looked like a dead end was providential design.

Both traditions take pastoral encouragement that God may lead his people into hard places for purposes they cannot yet see.

verses.text: They traveled from before Hahiroth, and crossed through the middle of the sea into the wilderness. They went three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham, and encamped in Marah.
verses.arminianNotes:
They passed through the sea into the wilderness, went three days in the wilderness of Etham, and camped at Marah. The great crossing is stated in a single line.

Arminian readers note the swift turn from triumph at the sea to bitter water at Marah, where trust was tested again (Exodus 15:22–26).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the crossing, the central saving act, is recorded with the same plainness as the stops. God’s mighty deeds are woven into ordinary days.

Both traditions recall Paul’s reflection that Israel passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), a warning and an encouragement for the church.

verses.text: They traveled from Marah, and came to Elim. In Elim, there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there.
verses.arminianNotes:
At Elim there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and they camped there. After Marah came refreshment.

Arminian readers see God’s kindness in providing rest after testing, a gift meant to strengthen trust for the road ahead.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the pattern of providence that mingles hardship and refreshment according to God’s wisdom (compare Exodus 15:27). He knows what his people need.

Both traditions take comfort that the wilderness includes oases, and that seasons of rest are gifts from God rather than accidents.

verses.text: They traveled from Elim, and encamped by the Red Sea.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Elim they camped by the Red Sea. This station is not mentioned in the Exodus narrative.

Arminian readers note that the list fills in details the narrative passed over, a reminder that much of daily faithfulness goes unrecorded in story form.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the itinerary and the narrative complement one another. Scripture does not tell everything, but what it tells is sufficient.

Both traditions treat the addition calmly and avoid speculating on the exact location of the camp.

verses.text: They traveled from the Red Sea, and encamped in the wilderness of Sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
From the Red Sea they camped in the wilderness of Sin. Exodus 16 places the first giving of manna and quail here.

Arminian readers recall the people’s complaints in this wilderness and God’s patient response, which invited trust rather than punishing at once.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers recall the manna as daily bread from heaven, a provision Jesus applied to himself as the true bread (John 6:31–35).

Both traditions see God’s faithful provision in a barren place, given even to a grumbling people.

verses.text: They traveled from the wilderness of Sin, and encamped in Dophkah.
verses.arminianNotes:
From the wilderness of Sin they camped at Dophkah. The name appears only in this list, and its location is unknown.

Arminian readers note that God accompanies his people through places that history has otherwise forgotten. Each stage required renewed obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s knowledge of his people is complete even where ours is not. A name we cannot place was known to him.

Both traditions find comfort that the ordinary, unremembered stretches of life are also under God’s care.

verses.text: They traveled from Dophkah, and encamped in Alush.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Dophkah they camped at Alush, another station known only from this list. Its site is likewise unidentified.

Arminian readers see in such quiet entries the daily walk of faith, where most steps are unremarkable but still matter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see providence at work in the small and unnamed details of life, not only in the dramatic moments.

Both traditions resist speculation about the location and instead draw from the text its simple witness: Israel kept moving, and God kept leading.

verses.text: They traveled from Alush, and encamped in Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink.
verses.arminianNotes:
At Rephidim there was no water for the people to drink. Exodus 17 tells of their quarrel with Moses and the water from the rock.

Arminian readers note that the people put the LORD to the test, a real failure of trust that Scripture later uses as a warning (compare Psalm 95:8–9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note Paul’s reading that the rock from which they drank was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). God supplied grace in the very place of complaint.

Both traditions see here both human unbelief and divine faithfulness, held together without excusing the first or diminishing the second.

verses.text: They traveled from Rephidim, and encamped in the wilderness of Sinai.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Rephidim they camped in the wilderness of Sinai. The list passes in a single line over the place where the covenant was given.

Arminian readers note that the people at Sinai entered a covenant with real obligations, to which they freely agreed (Exodus 24:3–8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the law was given to a people already redeemed. Grace preceded command, which shapes how both testaments relate law and gospel.

Both traditions see Sinai as a turning point in which God bound himself to Israel and called them to holiness.
